Subjects, methods, and results. Case 1. At age 53, the fa-
ther experienced episodic stiffness and discomfort in the right leg.
On two occasions, while driving, he had transient, involuntary
extension of his right leg. This necessitated removing his foot from
the automobile accelerator with his hand. One of these episodes
contributed to a minor motor vehicle accident. At neurologic eval-
uation 15 months after symptom onset, he had episodic right leg

history of pernicious anemia and thyroiditis. His family history
included type 1 diabetes, thyroiditis, and pernicious anemia (fig-
ure 1). Neurologic examination demonstrated episodic stiffening of
the right leg with knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion. The right
patellar muscle stretch reflex was disproportionately brisk and its
elicitation was followed immediately by prolonged spasm of the
quadriceps femoris. Plantar responses were flexor. There was no
lumbar hyperlordosis.

Case 2. His daughter’s initial symptom of SPS began at age
31 years. She experienced recurrent, episodic extension of her
head and neck. These episodes were initially brief, lasting only 2
to 3 seconds, and were provoked by anxiety and startle, but pro-
gressed over 6 years to last as long as 8 seconds. More severe
episodes were uncomfortable and associated with a transient
“tightness” in her throat that interfered with swallowing and
speaking. On examination, tapping of left or right patellar tendon
provoked opisthotonos lasting 4 to 6 seconds (see video E-1 at
www.neurology.org). This was more pronounced when the left pa-
tellar tendon was tapped while the patient was engaged in casual
conversation. The opisthotonic response abated when the patient
simultaneously performed mental arithmetic. Muscle stretch re-
flex testing elsewhere in the body did not elicit an abnormal re-
sponse. There was no lumbar hyperlordosis.
Surface electrodes recorded abnormally protracted motor unit
activity lasting up to 8 seconds following patellar tendon tapping
(figure 2). GAD65Ab values were 88.7 nmol/L and 95.6 nmol/L,
and thyroperoxidase antibody value was 100 IU/mL (normal /H1102120
IU/mL). She did not have clinical evidence of thyroiditis. Baclofen
relieved symptoms initially; it was gradually tapered and discon-
tinued as spontaneous opisthotonos became infrequent. However,
provocative maneuvers and anxiety continue to cause opisthoto-
nos, 48 months after initial presentation.
During this period, the daughter gave birth to a healthy infant
girl. Despite acquiring maternal GAD65 antibodies transplacen-
tally, the infant (now 3 years old) has not exhibited clinical symp-
toms or signs of SPS. Serial serum evaluations revealed GAD65Ab
values of 72.7 nmol/L at birth, 6.65 nmol/L at 3 months, and 0.65
nmol/L at 7 months.
Familial genetic and autoantibody investigation. With pro-
tocol approval by the Lahey Clinic Investigational Review Board
(LCID 2001–041), and the patient’s informed consent, we obtained
blood samples from the father, daughter, and nine other family
members (see figure 1). Serologic tests were performed for the
following autoantibodies: GAD65, thyrogastric, thyroid microso-
mal (peroxidase), gastric parietal cell, voltage-gated calcium chan-
nel N-type and P/Q-type, muscle acetylcholine receptor binding,
striated muscle, antinuclear (ANA), smooth muscle, mitochon-
drial, IA-2 islet cell, and neuronal cytoplasmic and nuclear anti-
bodies. Consistent with a hereditary predisposition to thyrogastric

MHC class II PCR/SSOP-based typing was performed for hu-
man leukocyte antigen (HLA) class II DRB1 and DQB1. The DNA
was extracted from blood and purified from 200 mL of blood using
QIA Amp DNA kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA). Between 50 and 100 ng
of genomic DNA was PCR amplified and typed for DRB1 and
DQB1 using immobilized sequence-specific oligonucleotide probes
in linear array format.
6,7 The HLA-DQB1*0201 and HLA-
DRB1*0301 alleles, which have previously been shown to be sus-
ceptibility alleles for SPS,
2,4 did not segregate with SPS in this
family. The father with SPS carried the DQB1*0201 allele but the
daughter did not. Neither carried the HLA-DRB1*0301 allele. The
father and daughter shared haplotypes DRB1*1303-DQB1*0301.
These haplotypes did not segregate with asymptomatic family

resent familial autoimmune SPS for the following
reasons: 1) each subject had episodic stiffness and
rigidity; 2) the father had painful spasms precipi-
tated by anxiety and relieved by diazepam and im-
munomodulatory therapy; 3) his daughter had
abnormal axial posture (opisthotonos) that was pre-
cipitated by tactile and emotional stimuli and re-
lieved by baclofen; 4) prolonged motor unit activity
was demonstrated electrophysiologically in the
daughter following tactile stimulation and was clini-
cally apparent in the father; 5) the GAD65Ab value
in both subjects exceeded 20 nmol/L; 6) the father
had clinical documentation of two coexisting autoim-
mune diseases and the daughter had serologic evi-
dence of thyroid autoimmunity; and 7) alternative
diagnoses were excluded.
GAD65Ab is characteristic but not specific for
SPS. High values (/H1102220.0 nmol/L) may be encoun-
tered in patients with polyendocrine autoimmunity.
5
However, the neurologic findings in both our pa-
tients were consistent with dysregulation of spinal or
supraspinal inhibitory circuits. We therefore con-
represents a biologic marker of SPS. Although
GAD65Ab was detected in four other family mem-
bers without SPS-like symptoms or signs, levels
were two log orders lower than the characteristic
threshold level for SPS, further supporting our con-
tention that GAD65 autoimmunity is related to the
neurologic disorders exhibited by the father and
daughter.
Our two familial cases of SPS had disparate clini-
cal presentations— one with asymmetric limb in-
volvement and the other intermittent, axial
involvement. Although neither subject had lumbar
hyperlordosis, a characteristic feature of SPS, this
does not develop in all patients and is frequently
absent early in the disease.
1,2 Furthermore, lumbar
hyperlordosis is usually absent in the stiff limb vari-
ant of SPS.
3 In our cases, the focal limb involvement
with early diagnosis and medical intervention in the
father and the intermittent nature of axial involve-
ment in the daughter provide explanations for the
absence of lumbar hyperlordosis. A judicious liberal-
ization of diagnostic criteria to accommodate the full
spectrum of SPS perhaps could permit earlier diag-
nosis and intervention aimed at preventing progres-
sion to a more severe phenotype.
Although intrathecal production of GAD65Ab oc-
curs in SPS,
8 the antigen’s location in the cytoplasm
of neurons suggests that this immunoglobulin G re-
flects rather than effects the pathogenic process in
SPS, as has been demonstrated for the type 1 Pur-
kinje cell cytoplasmic autoantibody marker of cere-
bellar ataxia.
9 The lack of abnormal neurologic signs
in the grandchild who acquired GAD65Ab transpla-
centally is consistent with GAD65Ab per se lacking
pathogenicity. However, it is instructive that even in
the instance of muscle acetylcholine receptor anti-
bodies of known pathogenicity in mothers who have
myasthenia gravis, only about 20% of infant recipi-
ents develop signs of neonatal myasthenia gravis.
The outcome in this instance is known to depend on
the fine specificity of the maternal antibodies.
10 It is
also possible that GAD65Ab may be accompanied by
an as yet unidentified effector autoantibody directed
at a neuronal plasma membrane component.
MHC II typing demonstrated that the HLA-
DQB1*0201 and DRB1*0301 alleles, which in white
subjects are considered susceptibility alleles for
SPS,
2,4 did not segregate with SPS in this family.
Because the data were derived from only one family
and the sample size is small, we cannot draw conclu-
sions from analysis of the shared haplotypes of fa-
ther and daughter (DRB1*1303-DQB1*0301), or of
the family members with evidence of autoimmunity.
